items.pronunciation_notes: उसने is two syllables with no vowel between स and न: us-ne.
items.gloss_en: the sentence that breaks everything you know

learn.title_en: वह खाता है, but उसने खाया
learn.explanation_en: Here is the whole difficulty of this module in one pair. वह खाता है is he eats — a plain subject, a verb agreeing with it, exactly as Module 7 taught. Put the same sentence in the perfective and it becomes उसने खाया: the subject has taken a marker ने, and the verb has stopped agreeing with it. Nothing else in Hindi does this. Every tense you learnt in Module 7 leaves the subject alone, and then the perfective arrives and rearranges the sentence.

examples.note: A plain subject, and the verb agrees with it — the ordinary pattern.
The subject now carries ने, and the verb no longer agrees with him.
The same shape with another verb — पीना behaves identically.

common_error.why_en: A transitive verb in the perfective needs ने on the subject. Leaving it out is the single most common Hindi error English speakers make.

practice.question: वह खाता है → ?
practice.explanation_en: The subject takes ने, and वह becomes उस before it — so उसने.

game.explanation_en: उसने खाया. ने is a postposition, so वह becomes the oblique stem उस and the two are written as one word.

items.pronunciation_notes: मैंने keeps the nasal from मैं before the ने: maiṁ-ne.

learn.explanation_en: ने is a postposition, so every pronoun in front of it behaves exactly as Module 6 taught: it goes oblique and fuses. मैं gives मैंने, तुम gives तुमने, वह gives उसने. There is nothing new to learn about the stems — उस is the same उस that gave you उसे and उसका. What is new is that a postposition is now attaching to the subject of the sentence, which is a place you have never seen one before.

examples.note: मैं plus ने, written as one word.
The habitual — no ने, and the verb agrees with मैं.
तुम plus ने, with the same fusion.

common_error.why_en: The pronoun and ने are written as one word, exactly as मुझे and उसका are.

practice.question: मैं देखता हूँ → ?
practice.explanation_en: मैं plus ने gives मैंने, written as one word.

game.explanation_en: मैंने देखा — one word, and मुझे would be the को form, which does a different job.

items.pronunciation_notes: Three separate words, with the marker रहा carrying the agreement: khaa ra-haa hai.
items.gloss_en: the boundary — every other tense is ने-free

learn.title_en: ने belongs to the perfective and nowhere else
learn.explanation_en: This is the single most useful fact in the module and it limits the damage enormously. ने appears only in the perfective. The habitual, the continuous, the future, the presumptive and every imperative are completely untouched — वह खाता है, वह खा रहा है, वह खाएगा, वह खाता होगा, खाओ. Not one of them takes ने. So of the nine cells in Module 7's grid plus the future and the imperatives, exactly one row is affected. If the sentence is not perfective, stop worrying.

examples.note: Continuous — no ने, and the verb agrees with वह.
Future — no ने either.
Perfective — the only place ने appears.

common_error.why_en: Over-applying ने is as common as forgetting it. The continuous never takes it, whatever the verb.

practice.question: खाना · वह · continuous present
practice.explanation_en: The continuous takes no ने. Only the perfective does.

game.explanation_en: Only the perfective. The habitual, continuous and future are all ने-free.

summary.recap_en: In the perfective, a transitive verb puts ने on its subject. ने is a postposition, so the pronoun in front of it goes oblique and fuses — मैंने, तुमने, उसने. And it appears in the perfective only: every other tense in the language leaves the subject alone.
summary.next_up_en: Next: exactly which sentences ने applies to, and one that looks like it should and does not.

items.pronunciation_notes: पढ़ा ends on a breathy flapped ṛh: pa-ṛhaa.

learn.title_en: The bare perfective takes ने too
learn.explanation_en: Module 7 showed that the perfective can stand with no auxiliary — वह आया, he came — and that this bare form is the ordinary past. The same is true with ने: उसने पढ़ा, he read. No auxiliary, and it is the form you will use most when telling someone what happened. Adding है or था gives you उसने पढ़ा है and उसने पढ़ा था, and ने stays put in all three because the aspect has not changed.

examples.note: The bare perfective, and the commonest form.
With है, and ने is still there.
With था, and ने is still there.

common_error.why_en: पढ़ना is transitive, so the perfective needs ने however short the sentence is.

practice.question: वह पढ़ता है → ?
practice.explanation_en: पढ़ना is transitive, so the perfective takes ने on the subject.

game.explanation_en: Only the perfective, whether or not an auxiliary follows it.

items.pronunciation_notes: किया is two light syllables with a य bridging them: ki-yaa.

learn.title_en: किया, दिया, लिया, पिया — now you can use them
learn.explanation_en: Module 7 taught four irregular perfective participles as recognition only: किया from करना, दिया from देना, लिया from लेना and पिया from पीना. All four are transitive, which is exactly why they were unusable — they needed ने, and ने had not arrived. Now it has. उसने किया, he did it; मैंने लिया, I took it. Nothing about the forms has changed; the missing piece was the construction they sit in.

examples.note: The participle from Module 7, now in the construction it needed.
लेना is transitive, so ने is required.
And देना behaves the same way.

common_error.why_en: This is the exact sentence Module 7 flagged as wrong. करना is transitive, so its perfective needs ने.

practice.question: मैं करता हूँ → ?
practice.explanation_en: मैंने किया — the irregular participle किया with ने on the subject.

game.explanation_en: उसने किया. करा is not the perfective of करना — किया is.

items.pronunciation_notes: Two light syllables with a य between: ga-yaa.

learn.title_en: ने is not a past marker
learn.explanation_en: वह गया is he went, in the perfective, with no ने anywhere — because जाना is intransitive. This matters more than it looks. Learners who meet ने first tend to treat it as a past tense marker and start attaching it to everything, and that produces उसने गया, which is wrong in a way that is immediately audible. ने marks the subject of a transitive verb. If the verb takes no object, there is no ने, whatever the tense. Levels nine and ten come back to this properly.

examples.note: Perfective, but जाना is intransitive so no ने.
आना is intransitive too, and the verb agrees with the subject.
खाना is transitive, so this one does take ने.

common_error.why_en: जाना is intransitive. ने marks the subject of a transitive verb and has nothing to do with tense.

practice.question: वह जाता है → ?
practice.explanation_en: जाना is intransitive, so no ने and the verb agrees with the subject.

game.explanation_en: Only खाना, because it is transitive. The other three verbs take no object.

summary.recap_en: ने needs two things at once: a perfective aspect and a transitive verb. Miss either and it does not appear. That is why वह गया has none and उसने खाया does, in the same tense. The four irregular participles from Module 7 are now fully usable.
summary.next_up_en: Next: the second half of the construction, and the part that surprises people more than ने itself.

levels.title_en: The verb agrees with the object

items.pronunciation_notes: खाई ends on two vowels running together: khaa-ii.
items.gloss_en: the verb follows the object, not the subject

learn.explanation_en: This is the part that surprises people more than ने does. Once ने is on the subject, the subject stops controlling the verb entirely — and the object takes over. उसने रोटी खाई has a feminine verb because रोटी is feminine, and it would be खाई whether the person eating were a man, a woman or a crowd. Every other construction in Hindi agrees with the subject. This one, and only this one, agrees with the object.

examples.note: खाई is feminine because रोटी is, not because of who ate it.
किताब is feminine, so पढ़ी.
चाय is feminine, and पीना gives पी in the feminine.

common_error.why_en: The verb agrees with रोटी, which is feminine. What the subject is makes no difference at all here.

practice.question: वह + रोटी + खाना · perfective
practice.explanation_en: ने on the subject, and the verb agrees with the feminine रोटी.

game.explanation_en: ने on the subject and पढ़ी agreeing with the feminine किताब.

items.pronunciation_notes: The noun and the verb rhyme, which is why the phrase sounds doubled: khaa-naa khaa-yaa.

learn.explanation_en: Change the object and the verb follows. खाना, food, is masculine, so उसने खाना खाया. The sentence looks doubled because the noun for food and the verb for eating come from the same root, and that is worth getting used to — खाना खाना is the ordinary way to say eat a meal. Compare it directly with उसने रोटी खाई from the last item: same subject, same verb, different object, different ending.

examples.note: खाना is masculine, so खाया.
पानी is masculine, so पिया rather than पी.
काम is masculine, so किया.

common_error.why_en: खाना is masculine. Once you start looking at the object it is easy to overcorrect and make everything feminine.

practice.question: वह + पानी + पीना · perfective
practice.explanation_en: पानी is masculine, so the verb is पिया.

game.explanation_en: काम is masculine and singular, so किया.

items.pronunciation_notes: Both words end on a nasal hum, which is what marks the feminine plural: roṭiyaaṁ khaa-iiṁ.

learn.title_en: The number follows the object too
learn.explanation_en: Agreement with the object means gender and number both. रोटियाँ is feminine plural, so the verb is खाईं with the nasal — the same nasalised feminine plural you met in Module 7 with वे गईं. So the object controls two things at once, and neither of them has anything to do with the subject. Four possible endings, exactly as with any perfective: खाया, खाई, खाए, खाईं.

examples.note: Feminine plural object, so the verb nasalises.
किताबें is feminine plural, so पढ़ीं.
सवाल is masculine plural, so the verb takes -ए.

common_error.why_en: The object is plural, so the verb nasalises. Dropping the hum makes it singular.

practice.question: वह + किताबें + पढ़ना · perfective
practice.explanation_en: किताबें is feminine plural, so the verb is पढ़ीं with the nasal.

game.explanation_en: सवाल here is masculine plural, so the verb takes -ए.

summary.recap_en: With ने on the subject, the verb agrees with the object in both gender and number: खाया, खाई, खाए, खाईं. This is the only construction in Hindi where the subject does not control the verb, and it is the half of the module that surprises people more than ने itself.
summary.next_up_en: Next: proof that the subject really is irrelevant, and what happens when the subject is a noun.

items.pronunciation_notes: With a noun subject, ने is written separately: laṛ-kii ne.
items.gloss_en: a feminine subject with a masculine verb

learn.title_en: A girl, and the verb is masculine
learn.explanation_en: This is the sentence that proves the rule. लड़की is unmistakably feminine, and the verb is खाया, masculine — because खाना is masculine and the subject has no say at all. If you find yourself wanting to write खाई here, that instinct is the whole reason this module exists. Note also that with a noun subject, ने is written as a separate word: लड़की ने, not लड़कीने. Only pronouns fuse with it.

examples.note: Feminine subject, masculine verb — the object decides.
पानी is masculine, so पिया, whoever drank it.
काम is masculine, so किया.

common_error.why_en: The verb agrees with खाना, which is masculine. That the subject is a girl changes nothing.

practice.question: लड़की + पानी + पीना · perfective
practice.explanation_en: पानी is masculine, so पिया — and ने is written separately after a noun.

game.explanation_en: काम is masculine, so किया. The subject being माँ makes no difference.

items.pronunciation_notes: लड़के is the oblique form, since ने is a postposition: laṛ-ke ne.
items.gloss_en: the mirror image, and the subject goes oblique

learn.explanation_en: Two things here. First, the mirror of the last item: a masculine subject with a feminine verb, because रोटी is feminine. Second, and easy to miss — the subject itself has gone oblique. लड़का becomes लड़के because ने is a postposition, and Module 6 taught that any noun in front of a postposition goes oblique. So a Class 1 subject changes shape before ने, and a plural subject becomes लड़कों ने. This catches people who are concentrating so hard on the verb that they forget the subject.

examples.note: Masculine subject, feminine verb — and लड़का has gone oblique.
A plural subject takes the oblique plural लड़कों.
Class 4, so the subject shows no change — but the verb is identical.

common_error.why_en: ने is a postposition, so a Class 1 noun in front of it goes oblique — exactly as it would before में or से.

practice.question: लड़का + रोटी + खाना · perfective
practice.explanation_en: The subject goes oblique before ने, and the verb agrees with the feminine रोटी.

game.explanation_en: Oblique subject before ने, and पढ़ी agreeing with the feminine किताब.

items.pronunciation_notes: Three nasal endings in one sentence — koṁ, beṁ and hiiṁ — and each is a hum.
items.gloss_en: everything plural, and none of it matching

learn.title_en: A plural masculine subject and a plural feminine verb
learn.explanation_en: This sentence has a masculine plural subject and a feminine plural verb, and both are correct. लड़कों is oblique plural because ने follows it; पढ़ीं is feminine plural because किताबें is. The two halves of the sentence are obeying different rules and neither is looking at the other. If you can build this one without hesitating, the core of the module is secure — everything after this level is about the cases where the pattern breaks.

examples.note: Oblique plural subject, feminine plural verb — two independent decisions.
Feminine plural subject, masculine singular verb.
बच्चा goes oblique plural to बच्चों before ने.

common_error.why_en: The verb follows किताबें, which is feminine plural. Matching it to the masculine subject is the instinct this module has to break.

practice.question: लड़कियाँ + खाना + खाना · perfective
practice.explanation_en: Oblique plural subject लड़कियों, and खाया agreeing with the masculine खाना.

game.explanation_en: Oblique plural बच्चों before ने, and पिया agreeing with the masculine पानी.

summary.recap_en: The subject's gender and number have no effect on the verb at all — लड़की ने खाना खाया and लड़के ने रोटी खाई prove it in both directions. And because ने is a postposition, the subject itself goes oblique in front of it: लड़के ने, लड़कों ने.
summary.next_up_en: Next: drinking and eating in conversation, where the object changes with every line.

items.pronunciation_notes: पी is a single long syllable, and it is the whole verb: pii.
items.gloss_en: पीना, whose feminine perfective is one syllable

learn.explanation_en: पीना is one of the four irregular perfectives, and its feminine form is simply पी — a single syllable that looks too short to be a verb. उसने चाय पी is he drank tea, and there is nothing missing. The full set is पिया, पी, पिए, पीं. Learners often add something to पी because it feels incomplete, and there is nothing to add. The same shortness turns up in की, the feminine of किया, which you met at the end of Module 7.

examples.note: चाय is feminine, so the verb is just पी.
दवा is feminine, and Hindi drinks medicine rather than taking it.
दूध is masculine, so the fuller form पिया.

common_error.why_en: The feminine of पिया is पी, with nothing after it. Adding a syllable to make it look like a verb is the usual instinct.

practice.question: वह + दवा + पीना · perfective
practice.explanation_en: दवा is feminine, so the verb is पी — one syllable and complete.

game.explanation_en: दूध is masculine, so पिया rather than पी.

items.pronunciation_notes: बनाया is three syllables with the length in the middle: ba-naa-yaa.
items.gloss_en: the Module 8 collocations, now in the past

learn.title_en: Everything you learnt in Module 8 now has a past
learn.explanation_en: Module 8 taught a great many collocations you could only use in the present — काम करना, खाना बनाना, दवा लेना, टिकट लेना, सवाल पूछना. All of them were stuck there because the verb was transitive. With ने they open up: मैंने खाना बनाया, मैंने दवा ली, उसने सवाल पूछा. Notice that the agreement follows the noun in the collocation, so दवा ली is feminine and खाना बनाया is masculine, and the pairs you memorised now carry their gender into the verb.

examples.note: खाना is masculine, so बनाया.
दवा is feminine, so ली — the feminine of लिया.
सवाल is masculine and singular here, so पूछा.

common_error.why_en: दवा is feminine — one of the -ा nouns Module 8 flagged — so the verb is ली.

practice.question: मैं + दवा + लेना · perfective
practice.explanation_en: दवा is feminine, so the verb is ली.

game.explanation_en: ने on the subject, and बनाया agreeing with the masculine खाना.

items.pronunciation_notes: The verb ends on two vowels running together: khaa-ii.

learn.title_en: The object changes on every line, and so does the verb
learn.explanation_en: Four ने sentences in a row, and the verb ending is different in three of them because the object is different each time. रोटी gives खाई, चाय gives पी, पानी gives पिया. The first line is worth a note: तुमने क्या खाया uses क्या as the object, and since क्या has no gender the verb falls back to the default masculine singular. That default is going to matter a great deal at level thirteen.

common_error.why_en: रोटी is feminine, so the verb is खाई — regardless of who is speaking.

practice.question: मैं + चाय + पीना · perfective
practice.explanation_en: चाय is feminine, so the verb is पी.

game.question_en: Listen to the second line. Which word is missing?
game.explanation_en: रोटी is feminine and singular, so the verb is खाई.

summary.recap_en: Every transitive collocation from Module 8 now has a past tense, and each one carries its noun's gender into the verb — खाना बनाया but दवा ली. When the object has no gender of its own, as with क्या, the verb falls back to masculine singular.
summary.next_up_en: Next: the full set of ने pronouns, including the one that catches everybody.
